chunks: And that which was narrated is: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Qasim from Aban from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdillah who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who married a woman, and he learned after marrying her that she had committed fornication. He said: 'If the husband wishes, he takes the dowry from the one who married her off, and she is entitled to the dowry for what he made lawful of her private part; and if he wishes, he leaves her.'
He said: 'And the woman is returned [from the marriage] due to leprosy, vitiligo, leprosy (skin disease), and madness; as for what is other than that, no [return is due].'

So this report is not contradictory to what we have presented, because he only said: if he learned that she had committed fornication, he has the right to claim the dowry from her guardian; and he did not say that he has the right to return her. Nor is it impossible that he has the right to reclaim the dowry even if he does not have the right to annul the contract, because one of the two rulings is separate from the other.

As for his saying 'as for what is other than that, no,' it does not indicate what we mentioned, that he does not have the right to return her merely due to fornication (moral corruption). Nor does it contradict what we presented that he has the right to return the lame, the one with a defect in her private part, and the blind.

Because these four things are among those from which he has the right to return her in all cases. And these other three things, even if he has the right to return her from them, it is better for him to keep her, and he does not return her from them.
As for the one with a defect in her private part, that which indicates that the man has the right to return her is what was narrated:

key_terms.الْمُفْضَاةُ: Woman with a defect in her private part

ai.seo_question: What are the husband's rights regarding dowry and annulment if his wife committed fornication before marriage?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the distinction between *khiyar al-ghabn* (option of defect) and *khiyar al-fusq* (option of moral fault), ruling that while a husband may reclaim the dowry (*sadaq*) from the guardian upon discovering prior fornication, he is not compelled to annul the marriage. This ruling highlights the Shia juristic principle that moral defects like fornication do not automatically invalidate the contract's stability, unlike physical defects such as lameness or blindness, where the husband retains the right to return the wife but is encouraged to keep her.
